Model verification for Edinburgh: forecasts made 1/3/5/7 days ahead vs ERA5 reanalysis, last 40 days (temp_mae in °C, lower is better; wet_dry_hit_pct = share of days the model got right whether it would rain over 1 mm). 'Claude (this page)' is your own previous forecasts, scored the same way (its rain call counts medium or high risk as rain); use its biases to correct yourself. 'station' is the same check against EGPH's own observed daily highs and lows (METAR; complete the next day, so it includes the last week that ERA5 hasn't reached; half-hourly integer readings, so its highs run a few tenths low)

Polar vortex strength: zonal-mean zonal wind at 60°N (m/s, daily UTC mean, positive = westerly) at 10 hPa (the standard SSW level: a reversal to easterly is a major sudden stratospheric warming) and 50 hPa (lower stratosphere), per model; ensembles give mean/p10/p90/min across members and the % of members easterly. Early-warning signs from the single runs: polar_cap_t10 = area-mean temperature over 60-90°N at 10 hPa (°C; a jump of 20 °C or more in a few days is a sudden warming under way), heat_flux_100 = eddy heat flux v'T' around 60°N at 100 hPa (K m/s; sustained high values push wave energy up and tend to weaken the vortex 1-2 weeks later), waves_10hPa = amplitude in metres of zonal wavenumber 1 and 2 in the 10 hPa geopotential height around 60°N (wave 1 growing to well over 1000 m means the vortex is being displaced off the pole; wave 2 growing to several hundred metres means it is being stretched towards a split; in winter a few hundred metres each is ordinary; waves_vs_season places today against this season's analysed days). wave2_by_level gives, per single run and day, the longitude (°E, 0-180; the second ridge is 180° further east) of the wave-2 ridges in the 60°N height at 500, 100 and 10 hPa, their amplitudes, and the tilt (10 hPa ridge minus 500 hPa ridge): a ridge that shifts west with height (negative tilt, e.g. 45°E at 500, 29°E at 100, 6°E at 10 hPa) with ridges near the Urals and Alaska is the structure of a split. For ensembles, pct_members_ever_easterly is the share of members that reverse on any day of the run (the SSW probability for that window; the per-day share understates it) and reversal_median_date the typical timing. Days before 2026-10-31 are analysis.

Arctic Oscillation (AO) and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) indices: last 10 days observed and NOAA CPC's GEFS forecast (31 members: mean/p10/p90/min/max, % negative). Negative AO/NAO favours blocking and cold spells in the UK; positive, mild westerlies.

Slow climate drivers: QBO (monthly equatorial zonal wind at 30 and 50 hPa, m/s; easterly QBO makes a weak vortex and SSWs more likely), ENSO (weekly Niño 3.4 SST anomaly and the ONI, °C; La Niña below -0.5, El Niño above +0.5, strong beyond ±1.5) and the MJO (last 10 days, Wheeler-Hendon phase 1-8 and amplitude; amplitude under 1 means weak). MJO phases 6-7 tend to favour a negative NAO 1-2 weeks later.

Positive = a cap higher than normal, i.e. a weak or displaced vortex; +1 sd at 100 hPa is the usual threshold for a stratospheric anomaly that couples to the surface (a negative AO/NAO in the following weeks), and +2 to +3 sd at 10 hPa is a major disturbance. periods.text: High pressure is set to dominate across the UK early in this period, bringing a lot of dry weather. Some places may start foggy, this slow to clear, possibly even lingering all day. Elsewhere, cloud amounts will be variable, but there should be some sunshine. Cloud may be thick enough at times for a little light drizzle though. For most, temperatures are likely to be close to normal for the time of year, though it will be chilly where any fog lingers. Some overnight frost is likely where skies are clear and winds remain light. As we head into the following week, there are signs that more unsettled weather may return, but confidence surrounding this change is low.

During the second half of November, there is an increasing chance of changeable or more unsettled conditions developing, which would mean spells of rain and the potential for strong winds at times. The extent and location of the wettest and/or windiest areas are very uncertain at this range, with the wettest and windiest weather probably towards the north and west, but there are hints that overall the south may be wetter than normal whilst the northwest is drier than normal, suggesting the possibility that areas of low pressure may be steered further south than normal. Overall, temperatures will probably be near or a little above normal for the time of year.

The next two weeks predicted ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies widespread across Europe this week will consolidate near Scandinavia next week favoring troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies initially limited to Southeastern Europe to expand across much of Southern and Central Europe. This pattern will favor normal to above normal temperatures widespread across most of Europe including the United Kingdom (UK) except for normal to below normal temperatures in the Balkan States and Turkey this week. However next week temperatures will become increasingly normal to below normal across much of Europe including the UK except for normal to above in Scandinavia and the Iberian Peninsula. The widespread warmth across the Northern Hemisphere (NH) this past summer and now the fall has continued into October (see Figure). However, a series of stretched polar vortex (PV) this month has led to some, albeit modest cooling in Siberia, East Asia and to an even lesser extent far Eastern Canada and New England (see Figure). However, one last stretched PV will bring more intense cooling to Siberia and East Asia and yet again more modest cooling to far eastern Canada and New England (see Figures 3 and 6). Some blocking in the North Atlantic and near Scandinavia will also bring colder temperatures to Europe (see Figure 9). But all eyes then turn to a much larger disruption of the PV that is likely to have an important influence on NH weather late November into December. Figure. Estimate of the observed surface temperatures (°C; shading) from 01 Oct to 25 Oct 2026 based on GFS initializations and the GFS forecast from the 13 Oct 2026 run.

I will spend most of the Impacts section discussing what is looking increasingly an unprecedented weak polar vortex (PV) for early November but a quick clarification about the super El Niño. I do believe that the super El Niño favors an overall mild winter for North America, especially eastern North America. The main reason because we have had a total of three super El Niños in the observational record and they all produced an overall mild winter. In fact, if my recollection is correct, all strong El Niños and La Niñas have produced relatively mild winters in the Eastern US. So maybe a more comprehensive conclusion is that all strong ENSO events favor a relatively mild winter in the Eastern US. But this certainly doesn't preclude more wintry periods that can even last multiple weeks. Where I think that I differ from most forecasters, I don’t think an overall mild winter is a foregone conclusion. And today’s blog is mostly about how uncertain the forecast is probably through the end of the year if not beyond. Figure i. With predicted negative geopotential height anomalies across Greenland (Figure 2), the NAO is predicted to be positive this week. Figure 1. The predicted daily-mean AO at a) 10 hPa and at b) 1000 hPa from the 00Z 26 Oct 2026 GFS ensemble. Gray lines indicate the AO index from each individual ensemble member, with the ensemble mean AO index given by the red line with squares. Ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies are predicted to dominate much of Europe with the exception of troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across troughing to the southeast across the Eastern Mediterranean this week (Figure 2). This pattern will support widespread normal to above normal temperatures across much of Europe including the UK except for normal to below normal temperatures across the Balkans and Turkey this week (Figure 3). Forecasted average 500 mb geopotential heights (dam; contours) and geopotential height anomalies (m; shading) across the Northern Hemisphere from 1 Nov to 5 Nov 2026. The forecasts are from the 00Z 26 Oct 2026 GFS ensemble. Ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies centered between the UK and Scandinavia will support deepening troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across the Southeastern Europe this period (Figure 5). The pattern will support widespread normal to above normal temperatures across Europe including the UK except for normal to below normal temperatures across the Mediterranean countries and possibly into Central Europe this period (Figure 6). Ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies centered Northern Europe and the Barents-Kara Seas will support troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across Siberia and into Northeast Asia this period (Figure 5). This pattern favors widespread normal to above normal temperatures widespread across Western and Southern Asia but especially South-Central Asia with normal to below normal temperatures across Si [...]

With predicted weak but positive pressure/geopotential height anomalies across Greenland (Figure 8), the NAO will likely turn negative this period as well. Figure 8. Forecasted average 500 mb geopotential heights (dam; contours) and geopotential height anomalies (m; shading) across the Northern Hemisphere from 6 Nov to 10 Nov 2026. The forecasts are from the 00Z 26 Oct 2026 GFS ensemble. Ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies are predicted to persist across Scandinavia and the Barents-Kara Seas and this will promote deepening troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies to the south across Central and Southern Europe this period (Figure 8). This pattern will favor expanding normal to below normal temperatures across much of Europe including the UK with the exception of normal to above normal temperatures in the Iberian Peninsula and Scandinavia this period (Figures 9). It has been shown that less sea ice in the North Atlantic sector of the Arctic weakens the polar vortex while less sea ice in the North Pacific sector strengthens the polar vortex. Sea ice has been growing a good clip, but more in the but North Pacific sector than the North Atlantic sector and therefore Arctic sea ice anomalies continue to show a strong focus or weighting of negative anomalies towards the North Atlantic sector relative to the North Pacific sector and this is a robust signal of an overall weaker PV this winter. analysis.headline: No warnings are in force. Halloween stays dry and mild, then a strong high over Scotland brings a week of calm, foggy, grey weather, with rain returning around 9-10 November. Overhead, the polar vortex is forecast to reverse around 5 November in every ECMWF and Canadian ensemble member.
analysis.summary: At 08:50 UTC Edinburgh Airport had 9 °C (dew point 8 °C), a light westerly, clear skies (CAVOK) and 1030 hPa. There was fog nearby at 07:20 and a low of 7 °C, matching the hourly guidance. Halloween is dry and mild, near 14.5 °C. The weak front tonight now gives no measurable rain, just a gustier south-westerly and cloud. Sunday is fresher and bright. From Monday a 1033-1039 hPa high sits over Scotland, centred over the north-east by Thursday 5 November in ECMWF and ICON. That means calm, often foggy or grey days near 10 °C, a chilly first half of Monday night, and possible drizzle from low cloud on 3 and 6 November. Around 8-10 November the high drifts towards Scandinavia and Atlantic lows push in from the south-west: ECMWF HRES has a deep low south-west of Ireland by 10 November, and the ensembles have a more than 1 mm chance of 45-57% a day on 10-13 November. In the stratosphere the 60°N 10 hPa wind is 12.3 m/s, just above NASA's record low for the date (11.3 m/s). Every ECMWF ENS and GEPS member and 90% of GEFS reverse it to easterly around 5 November. On the 100 hPa polar cap the event is deep (+1.8 sd now, peaks +2.1 to +2.4 sd); on the 50 hPa wind it is not (westerly throughout).

The high strengthens to the north (1036-1039 hPa). Dry and calm, with fog or low cloud slow to clear near the Forth and some brightness elsewhere. About 10.5 °C; chilly where fog lingers. The chance of more than 1 mm is 2% in ECMWF ENS and AIFS ENS, 0% in GEFS.

Bonfire Night. The high is centred over north-east Scotland (1038-1039 hPa in ECMWF and ICON), so it stays still and mostly dry. Fog and firework smoke may be trapped in the evening (sunset 16:24), about 7-8 °C. No ECMWF ENS member gives more than 1 mm. ICON's deterministic run (1.9 mm, gusts 45 km/h) is an outlier.
days.wind: Light E-SE 5-12 km/h, gusts up to about 25 km/h

days.summary: The high drifts towards the North Sea and Norway and the flow turns south-easterly: grey with low cloud and the odd spot of drizzle. The chance of more than 1 mm is 4% in ECMWF ENS but 22-42% in AIFS ENS, ICON-EPS, GEM ENS and AIGEFS, so drizzle is plausible but light. Mild nights under cloud, about 10 °C by day.

medium_range.summary:
From 7 to 16 November the block weakens and slides east, and the Atlantic returns from the south-west.

On 7 November ECMWF HRES has 1030 hPa over eastern Scotland, with pressure falling to the south-west. JMA has the high over the North Sea and Germany, with a 995 hPa low west of Iberia. AIFS and GEM keep 1026-1030 hPa nearby.

By 10 November the runs diverge:
- ECMWF HRES drives a deep low (about 970 hPa) south-west of Ireland, with a strong south to south-east gradient over Scotland (gusts 46 km/h on 9 November).
- JMA has a 985 hPa low west of Ireland.
- GEM and AIFS (machine learning) are gentler, with a south to south-west flow and 1016-1018 hPa over Edinburgh.
- The ECMWF ENS and GEFS means both put a trough just west of the UK (552 dam line west of Ireland).

By 15 November the GEFS mean has a broad westerly with the 552 dam line over northern Scotland. The AIFS deterministic run has a deep low over Norway, which would mean a chilly north-westerly. The AIFS ENS spread over the UK reaches 12-18 hPa, so confidence is low.

At the point, the 850 hPa means stay near 0 to +2 °C:
- ECMWF ENS: -0.4 to -0.7 °C on 7-9 November.
- GEFS: the coldest, -1.5 °C on 7-8 November.
- GEM ENS: the mildest, about +2 °C.
- The 10th percentiles reach -4 to -5.7 °C on 12-14 November.

All ensembles agree on a wetter turn. The chance of more than 1 mm a day on 10-13 November is 39-57% in ECMWF ENS and 45-55% in GEFS. Expect highs of 8-10 °C and lows of 3-6 °C. Beyond day 7 I weight the ensembles over single runs.
signals: Dry and settled with high confidence to 6 November, then low drizzle risk. ECMWF HRES stays near dry to 8 November, with highs falling to about 8-9 °C on 7-9 November.

Rain from about 9-10 November. ECMWF ENS mean 6-hourly totals rise to 0.6-1.1 mm on 10-14 November.
- Wettest members: ECMWF ENS up to 19-20 mm a day on 11 and 13 November.
- GEFS maximum 27 mm on 13 November.
- GEM ENS 90th percentile 9.2 mm in 6 hours on 8 November.
Wind: ECMWF HRES gusts 46 km/h on 9 November with the deep low to the south-west. The EPSgram shows mean wind speeds edging above the model median from 9-10 November.

Snow (850 hPa at or below -5 °C while 0.5 mm falls), share of members:
- ECMWF ENS: 0% every day, down from 2-4% last run.
- GEFS: 0%.
- AIFS ENS: 4% on 14 November.
- GEM ENS: 5% on 9 November.
Open-Meteo snowfall: GEFS 3% on 9 November and 6% on 13 November; AIFS ENS 2% on 10 and 14 November. Lying snow in ECMWF ENS: 0%. Any snow would be on the Pentlands only.
Frost and ice: ECMWF ENS frost 6-8% a day on 11-13 November; ice (frost on a wet day) 2-4% on 7 and 10-12 November; AIGEFS ice 3% on 11, 12 and 14 November.

AO and NAO (NOAA GEFS, 30 October): the AO falls from +0.95 to about -1.4 on 6-13 November, with 81-100% of members negative. The NAO goes from +1.1 to -0.5 on 6 November and -1.0 to -1.06 on 11-13 November, with 90% of members negative.

Hovmöller (30 October run): a ridge at about 0° to 3-4 November. A deep trough at 25-50°E from about 4 to 14 November, strongest on 6-10 November: a ridge-west, trough-east (northerly) set-up for Europe. Most runs keep the UK on the ridge's Atlantic side in south-easterlies, though, so it mainly chills central and eastern Europe (ECMWF week-2 map: -1 to -3 °C there).

Upwind cold is building east but thin (ECMWF ENS, by 11-14 November, members at -8 °C at 850 hPa):
- Stockholm 2-8%, Oslo 0-4%, Copenhagen 0%.
- Helsinki 14-24%.
- Moscow 39-49%, but it lies south-east of our usual track.
Scandinavian snow cover is 0-6% of members, so an easterly would be raw and grey rather than snowy.

Angular momentum (AAM) is +1.44 sd, down 0.87 in 7 days. The Global Wind Oscillation (GWO) is in phase 7 (amplitude 2.0): the high-AAM state turning down, which often brings mid-latitude ridging 1-2 weeks later. It fits the current block; background only.

models.view: Dry to 6 November apart from 0.6 mm on 3 November, with highs of 9.5-11 °C. Its highs run about 1 °C too cool here. 1039 hPa over north-east Scotland on 5 November. It is the deepest with the 10 November low south-west of Ireland (around 970 hPa), with 46 km/h gusts on 9 November. Its 10 hPa wind turns easterly on 5 November.

Dry to 8 November (0-12% chance of more than 1 mm a day), with 850 hPa +2 to +4 °C under the inversion on 3-6 November. The chance of more than 1 mm rises to 31% on 9 November and 45-57% on 10-13 November. The mean 850 hPa is +1 to +2 °C on 10-14 November with a wide spread (10th percentile to -5.2 °C). No snow members, no lying snow, frost at most 8%. The 10 November mean has a trough west of Ireland.

The deterministic run has 1036 hPa just north on 5 November, 1026 hPa to the west on 7 November with 850 hPa about -1 °C over western Scotland, and a south-westerly on 10 November. By 15 November it has a deep low over Norway with the UK in a cold north-westerly, colder than the physics ensembles. The ensemble mean is slightly wetter than ECMWF ENS from 5 November (12-25% a day), with very large spread over the UK by 15 November.

The wettest physics model on 3 November (1.8 mm; 39% of members give more than 1 mm). Otherwise similar, with highs of 9-11 °C. Its lows have run about 1 °C too warm at ERA5 grid level and 1.7 °C too warm against the airport.

The deterministic run is dry throughout with mild lows of 7-9 °C (lows bias +2 °C against the airport). GEFS is the coldest point ensemble on 7-9 November (mean 850 hPa about -1.5 °C) and wet from 10 November (45-55%). The mean on 15 November is a westerly with the 552 dam line over northern Scotland.
The coolest highs (6.8-9.4 °C), consistent with its -1.3 °C bias on highs. AIGEFS is the wettest ensemble early, at 29-45% on 5-7 November.

The best recent scores and the top blend weight. Dry and calm to 4 November, then 1.9 mm with gusts of 45 km/h on 5 November, wetter and windier than everyone else. ICON-EPS gives 8% that day, so I treat it as an outlier.

1038 hPa over Scotland on 5 November and 1030 hPa on 7 November, then a mild southerly (850 hPa +4 to +5 °C) on 10 November. GEM ENS is the wettest and mildest ensemble (29-57% a day from 3 November). The deterministic run's 0.9 °C low on 2 November is the coldest.

JMA and NAVGEM put the 5 November high centre over the North Sea (1035 hPa). JMA has a 995 hPa low west of Iberia on 7 November and 985 hPa west of Ireland on 10 November, close to ECMWF HRES. ARPEGE is dry and mild to 3 November, in line with the others.

extended_range.summary:
The ECMWF extended products are now from the 30 October run.

Edinburgh weekly meteogram (medians):
- 2 m temperature: about 0 °C for the week to 9 November, about +0.5 °C to 16 November, near +1 °C for 16-23 November, then +0.3 to +0.5 °C into mid-December.
- Precipitation: clearly below normal to 9 November and near to slightly below to 16 November. Near normal or slightly above after that.
- Pressure: far above normal in the first week, then near or slightly below normal.

Weekly maps:
- 9-16 November: a 500 hPa ridge from Greenland down over the UK to the Mediterranean, a trough over Scandinavia and western Russia, and a surface high anomaly over Norway and the North Sea with low pressure west of Iberia. That gives Edinburgh about 0 to +1 °C and a light south-easterly to easterly drift, while central and eastern Europe is 1-3 °C colder than normal.
- 23-30 November: a trough west of Ireland and over Scandinavia, with low pressure over the UK. Changeable and slightly mild.
- 7-14 December: positive heights over Greenland, a weak trough near Ireland and a high over North Africa, a weak NAO- shape with near-normal temperatures.

Hovmöller (35-60°N):
- 25-50°E column: a trough from about 4 to 14 November (strongest 6-10 November), and a weaker one around 21-25 November.
- 0° column: ridging returns around 13-22 November.
- So a ridge-west, trough-east window runs about 5-13 November, but most runs keep the UK on the mild, Atlantic side of the ridge.

Met Office long-range text (4-28 November): high pressure with fog and frost, near-normal temperatures, then increasingly unsettled in the second half, with lows steered south (south wetter, north-west drier) and near or slightly above-normal temperatures. I agree with the first half, but I bring the change forward a little, to about 9-10 November, because the ECMWF HRES, JMA and ensemble means all bring an Atlantic trough in. The southward-steered storm track fits GEFS's NAO near -1. That is why I give 16-30 November only a slight mild lean despite NAO+ leading ECMWF's regimes.

Judah Cohen's AER post (26 October, 5 days old) expects the AO and NAO to turn negative in week 2 and normal to below-normal temperatures over much of Europe, including the UK. The AO and NAO part is verifying in the forecasts. For the UK, the ECMWF weeklies keep Edinburgh near or slightly above normal, so I differ on the temperature.

The seasonal maps are from runs started on 1 October, before this vortex event, which they do not include:
- C3S November-December: +0.5 to +1 °C for the UK.
- SEAS5 and GloSea December-February: mild.

weeks.pattern: A strong blocking high over Scotland and the North Sea: dry, calm, foggy and grey, with chilly clear nights. It drifts towards Norway from about 7 November.

The Atlantic Ridge leads ECMWF's regimes (about 40-58%) as the NAO turns negative (GEFS about -1). High pressure over Scandinavia meets Atlantic lows to the south-west, giving south-easterly rain and wind from about 9-10 November. A cold north-westerly in a minority (AIFS). Hill snow only in a few members.
NAO+ becomes ECMWF's largest regime (30-37%), with Atlantic westerlies. Simon Lee's index keeps a slight NAO- lean, and the Met Office hints at lows steered south, so the mild lean is weak.
Mixed regimes (NAO+ about 22-26%, NAO- about 18-21%, blocking about 13-18%) with a trough over and west of the UK: changeable, rain at times, slightly mild.
Blocking climbs to lead at about 34-41% on 3-7 December, a possible delayed response to the stratospheric event, with NAO+ still about 20%.
Weak positive heights over Greenland with low pressure near the UK: a weak NAO- shape favouring a southern storm track and occasional northerlies.

extended_range.regimes:
ECMWF regime probabilities (30 October run):
- Blocking: 100% to 3 November, 90-97% to 5 November, 65% on 6 November and 48% on 7 November.
- Atlantic Ridge: leads on 8-14 November, peaking about 58% on 9 November.
- NAO+: grows to be the largest regime on 17-24 November (about 30-37%), with NAO- only 9-12%.
- Late November: mixed, with NAO- rising to about 20% from 25 November.
- Blocking: leads again on 3-7 December (about 34-41%), the highest beyond week 2 so far.

Simon Lee's index (29 October run; a different scheme, so compare timing only):
- Scandinavian blocking at +2 sd to about 5 November, decaying to zero by about 10 November.
- Atlantic Ridge peaking on 2-3 November.
- NAO+ about -1.6 sd on 4-5 November.
- NAO- rising to about +0.6 sd by 9 November and staying +0.4 to +0.6 sd into December.

The two agree on the block breaking down around 7-10 November. They disagree on 17-24 November, when ECMWF leans NAO+ and Lee's index still leans NAO-. The GEFS NAO of about -1 on 10-14 November sides with Lee for the first part.

For Edinburgh: a dry, grey first week; a wetter, south-easterly-tinged second week; a changeable, slightly mild late November; and a better-than-usual chance of a blocked spell in early December.

stratosphere.summary:
Strength now: the 60°N 10 hPa wind is 12.3 m/s (ECMWF analysis; GFS 11.5-12.2 m/s). Against NASA's 1979-2026 climatology for 31 October it is far below the 10th percentile (17.6 m/s) and only 1 m/s above the record minimum (11.3 m/s); the mean is 24.2 m/s. Severe-weather.eu calls it weaker than 9 years in 10, and weatheriscool's ERA5 weakest for the date is 11.6 m/s (2016). At 50 hPa the wind is 7.7-8.0 m/s, at the NASA record minimum for the date (7.5 m/s).

Early-warning signs fired strongly:
- The 100 hPa heat flux at 60°N peaked at 46-48 K m/s on 29 October, with a second pulse of 38-41 K m/s on 3 November.
- On severe-weather.eu (45-75°N) it is 24.2 K m/s now against a mean of 10.5 and a 90th percentile of 16.8, peaking at 28.6 on 2 November.
- NASA's 45-day mean is above its 90th percentile.
- The flux then collapses to 4-17 K m/s by 9-12 November.
- The 10 hPa polar-cap temperature rises only 4-6 °C, to -55 to -57 °C on 8 November, but that is above the 1958-2025 maximum for those dates.

Reversal:
- The ECMWF ENS mean turns easterly on 5 November and bottoms at -4.0 m/s on 10 November; 39% of members are still easterly on 14 November.
- GEOS-FP goes easterly on 5 November, to -5.0 m/s on 8 November.

Shape: on 1-2 November wave 2 peaks at 578-607 m in every model. In ECMWF its ridges tilt west with height: the 500 hPa ridge is at 35-41°E (Urals), the 10 hPa ridge at about 5°E, and the partner ridge 180° away near Alaska, a tilt of -30° to -36°. That is the structure of a split.
- The hebweather GFS, ECMWF and GEFS comparison for 4 November and the NOAA GFS map at +120 h both show two lows, over Canada and over the Siberian Arctic: split-like.
- After that, wave 2 collapses (60-100 m by 10-12 November) and wave 1 grows to 758-794 m by 12-15 November. The ECMWF centroid is at 60-63°N to 10 November. That is a displacement towards the Atlantic side.
- The ECMWF 10 hPa maps put the low over Hudson Bay on 5 November and over Greenland and Baffin on 10 November. The ECMWF ENS mean, GFS and NOAA +384 h maps centre it over Scandinavia and the Barents Sea by 15-16 November.
- The machine-learning AIFS 10 hPa maps (Europe sector only) put the cold core over Greenland, Iceland and Scandinavia on 5-10 November and over the Barents Sea by 15 November. That is consistent with a displaced, not split, vortex.

Depth: the two measures disagree.
- 100 hPa polar-cap height: +1.76 sd now. Deterministic peaks are ECMWF HRES +2.44, GFS +2.31, UKMO +2.24, GEM +2.12 and AIFS +2.07 sd. 100% of members in ECMWF ENS, AIFS ENS, GEFS and GEPS reach +1 sd. On this measure the event is deep.
- 50 hPa wind: stays westerly. Ever easterly there are 2% of ECMWF ENS, 0% of GEFS, 0% of AIFS ENS and 3% of AIGEFS, with deterministic minima of +2.3 to +5.2 m/s. The GFS section takes easterlies only down to 20-30 hPa on 5 November.

The deep cap lasts longer in some ensembles than others. Share of members still above +1 sd at 100 hPa:
- ECMWF ENS: 51% on 13 November, 45% on 14 November.
- AIFS ENS: 84% on 14 November.
- GEPS: 57% on 16 November.
- GEFS: 16% from 13 November.

Further down, coupling is modest. The 500 hPa cap peaks at +0.94 sd in ECMWF HRES and +1.29 in GFS on 7 November; the GFS section's 1000 hPa cap reaches +0.86 on 7 November, then all fall to near zero by 9-10 November.

models.view: 12.3 m/s now. Easterly from 5 November, weakest -4.3 m/s on 10 November, back to +3.4 m/s by 14 November. Split-type wave 2 first, then displaced towards Greenland and Scandinavia (wave 1 at 758 m on 14 November). 50 hPa minimum 2.6 m/s; 100 hPa cap peak +2.44 sd on 7 November.

11.5 m/s now. Easterly on 4-5 November (weakest -1.3 m/s), then hovering at +0.3 to +3 m/s to 16 November. Easterlies reach 30 hPa. 50 hPa minimum 2.3 m/s. 100 hPa cap peak +2.31 sd; 500 hPa +1.29 and 1000 hPa +0.86 sd on 7 November, stronger surface coupling than yesterday.

The least disturbed run: it stays westerly, weakest 3.6 m/s on 9 November and back to about 12 m/s by 14-15 November. A strong displacement (wave 1 at 794 m). 50 hPa minimum 4.0 m/s; 100 hPa cap +2.07 sd, fading to +0.26 sd by 14 November. It is less disturbed than the physics models.
Easterly from 5 November at the 10 hPa level the run carries, weakest -0.8 m/s on 9 November at the end of its run. 100 hPa cap peak +2.12 sd; 50 hPa minimum 3.1 m/s.
Bottoms at 1.1 m/s on 5 November at the end of its run, just short of reversing. 100 hPa cap peak +2.24 sd; 50 hPa minimum 3.1 m/s.
2.9 m/s on 3 November at the end of its run, falling in step with the others.
50 hPa minimum 3.0 m/s on 4 November; no 10 hPa data.
50 hPa minimum 5.2 m/s, the least disturbed in the lower stratosphere.

100% of members easterly on some day (numeric data), median first reversal 5 November, 98% easterly on 8-10 November and 39% still easterly on 14 November. Mean minimum -4.0 m/s, lowest member -10.0 m/s. 2% easterly at 50 hPa. 100 hPa cap: all members above +1 sd, 45% still there on 14 November. Weatheriscool quotes 69%, evidently a different run or window; severe-weather.eu has 100%. I use 100%.

00Z 31 October: 90% of members easterly on some day (up from 77%), median 5 November, 77% on 5 November. A dip to 6% on 7 November, a second peak of 55% on 12 November, and 3% by 14-16 November. 0% at 50 hPa. The 100 hPa cap peaks at +2.08 sd, but only 16% of members are above +1 sd from 13 November, the quickest recovery.

51% of members easterly on some day (severe-weather.eu has 59% to 15 November), down from 73%. Median 5 November, peak 37% on 10 November, lowest member -4.4 m/s. 0% at 50 hPa. Yet 84% of members are still above +1 sd on the 100 hPa cap on 14 November: weaker at 10 hPa but more persistent lower down than the physics ensembles.
No 10 hPa data. The 50 hPa mean falls to 2.6 m/s; 3% of members turn easterly there on 11 November (down from 23%).

100% of members easterly, median 5 November, 90-95% easterly on 5-6 November and 10-11 November, still 43% on 16 November. Mean minimum -2.2 m/s, lowest member -8.0 m/s. 10 hPa cap peak +4.94 sd; 100 hPa cap +2.28 sd, with 57% of members above +1 sd on 16 November. The most disturbed and most persistent ensemble.

My reading of the chart: all members fall to about 0 m/s by 5 November, essentially every member is below zero at some time on 8-15 November, and the mean is about -2 to -3 m/s around 10-11 November. The lowest member is about -11 m/s around 19 November. That matches the numeric 100% from the 31 October ENS. The mean regains zero around 15-17 November, reaches the model-climate mean (about 32 m/s) around 28-30 November and about 42 m/s by 14 December, above normal. The weekly 10 hPa maps show Siberian-side warmth on 2-9 November, warmth over Canada and Greenland on 16-23 November, and a cold, re-centred pole on 30 November-7 December.

hazards.what: Fog, locally dense and slow to clear near the Forth under a 1036-1039 hPa high, with grey, damp gloom. No Met Office warnings are in force.

hazards.when: Evening Mon 2 Nov into early Tue 3 Nov
hazards.what: A chilly clear spell before cloud arrives: about 3 °C at the airport, with ground frost possible in rural hollows and on untreated surfaces.
Very light winds under the high centre may trap fog and firework smoke, cutting visibility and air quality locally. Dry in most models.

Rain at times as Atlantic lows push in from the south-west, with a strong south to south-east breeze (ECMWF HRES gusts to 46 km/h on 9 November). The wettest members give 15-27 mm in a day. Ice on wet nights: 2-4% of ECMWF ENS members. Snow showers on the Pentlands in a few members (2-6%); city snow and lying snow 0% in ECMWF ENS.

A colder, blocked spell is more likely than usual as the vortex disruption couples down (NAO forecast near -1 by 10-13 November; ECMWF blocking about 40% on 3-7 December). The main risks are frost, ice and hill snow; lowland snow needs cold air over Scandinavia first, which is not there yet.

analysis.changes_since_last:
Short range unchanged: dry and mild to Halloween, then a foggy high on 2-6 November. Yesterday verified at 15 °C. Changes since the last analysis:
- Halloween's spot of drizzle has gone; the hourly guidance is dry.
- The high is now centred over north-east Scotland on 5 November in ECMWF and ICON.
- Drizzle risk on 6 November has risen in AIFS ENS, GEM ENS and AIGEFS.
- Medium range: ECMWF HRES and JMA now bring a deep Atlantic low south-west of Ireland by 10 November, so the wet, breezy turn around 9-10 November is firmer, with south-easterlies rather than AIFS's cold north-westerly.
- Snow: ECMWF ENS snow members fell from 2-4% to 0%.
- Upwind cold eased: Stockholm's share of members at -8 °C is down from 14% to 8%, Oslo from 6% to 4%.
- ECMWF extended products updated to the 30 October run: Atlantic Ridge on 8-14 November, NAO+ largest on 17-24 November, and blocking stronger in early December (about 40% against 26-35% before).

Stratosphere:
- NASA's climatology loaded this run: the 10 hPa wind is just above the record low for the date, and the 50 hPa wind is at its record low.
- GEFS reversal share rose from 77% to 90% in the new 00Z run.
- AIFS ENS fell from 73% to 51%, and the AIFS deterministic minimum rose to 3.6 m/s.
- ECMWF ENS is still 100%, slightly deeper (mean -4.0 m/s, lowest member -10.0 m/s), but recovers a little sooner (39% easterly on 14 November).
- ECMWF HRES now recovers to +3.4 m/s by 14 November.
- The 50 hPa wind stays westerly everywhere (AIGEFS easterly share down from 23% to 3%).
- The 100 hPa cap is still deep. GFS surface coupling is slightly stronger again (1000 hPa cap +0.86 sd on 7 November, against +0.5-0.6).

chart_notes.note: ECMWF HRES +120 h (5 Nov): 1039 hPa high centred over north-east Scotland. Calm, still air: fog and trapped Bonfire Night smoke.
ECMWF HRES +240 h (10 Nov): a deep low (about 970 hPa) south-west of Ireland with a tight south-easterly gradient over Scotland. The wettest and windiest solution.
ECMWF ENS mean +240 h: a trough with the 552 dam line just west of Ireland. The Atlantic is back in by 10 November.
ECMWF EPSgram: dry to 8 November, precipitation boxes growing from 9-10 November, temperatures close to the model climate.
ECMWF regimes (30 Oct): blocking to 6 November, Atlantic Ridge on 8-14 November, NAO+ largest on 17-24 November, blocking back to about 40% on 3-7 December.
ECMWF weekly 500 hPa for 9-16 November: a ridge from Greenland over the UK and a trough over Scandinavia and Russia. Cold for central and eastern Europe, near normal here.
Hovmöller: a trough at 25-50°E from 4 to 14 November (strongest 6-10 November), ridging at 0° around 13-22 November, and a second weak eastern trough around 21-25 November.
Simon Lee's index: Scandinavian blocking fades to zero by about 10 November; NAO- stays slightly positive into December, unlike ECMWF's NAO+ lean on 17-24 November.
ECMWF 46-day 10 hPa wind: essentially every member below zero on 8-15 November, a recovery to the model-climate mean by about 28-30 November and above normal by mid-December.
GFS polar-cap 'dripping paint' chart: +2 to +2.4 sd at 100 hPa on 2-7 November, reaching +1 sd near 500 hPa and +0.9 sd near the surface on 7 November, then fading.
Reversal shares: ECMWF ENS 100%, GEFS 90% and AIFS ENS 59% by 15-16 November; ECMWF ENS peaks at 100% on 9-10 November.
GFS, ECMWF and GEFS 10 hPa heights at +96 h (4 Nov): two lows, over Canada and the Siberian Arctic. A split-like shape before the vortex displaces towards Greenland and Scandinavia.
ECMWF weekly MSLP for 9-16 November: high over Norway and the North Sea, low west of Iberia, so a south-easterly regime for Scotland.

winter_outlook.summary:
My call is a near-normal to slightly mild winter overall, wetter than average in December. I expect chilly, blocked spells in November and a cold tilt in late winter, but not a cold winter as a whole. Confidence is low.

The odds:
- December-February colder than its 1991-2020 normal: 27% (medium, near the bottom of the band).
- At least one proper cold spell between November and March (5 or more days in a row each with a minimum of -3 °C or lower, or 5 cm of snow lying): 44% (medium).
- A major stratospheric warming starting in November: 92%; December 8%; January 15%; February 20%.

The big event is real and has firmed up. The polar vortex is collapsing in the first week of November, something not seen in any autumn since 1979. Every ECMWF and Canadian ensemble member, and 90% of the American ones, reverse the 60°N wind by about 5 November. NASA's own GEOS forecast goes to -5 m/s by 8 November, and high pressure fills the polar cap down to 100 hPa.

That pushes the cold-spell odds up a little. It does much less for December-February, for three reasons:
- The models rebuild the vortex to above-normal strength by early to mid-December.
- A westerly QBO helps that rebuild.
- A super El Niño and a westerly-favouring Atlantic sea-temperature pattern both lean towards mild, wet Decembers.

The best cold chances, in order:
- Frost and fog under high pressure on 3-16 November, turning to a cool north-westerly drift. Snow is likely on the Pentlands, the city stays frosty rather than snowy.
- Late November to early December, if the stratospheric signal reaches the surface.
- February.

The missing ingredient for snow in the city is still cold air over Scandinavia. At most 4% of ECMWF members bring -8 °C air at 850 hPa to Oslo by 14 November, and 8% to Stockholm. The ground there is bare.
winter_outlook.reasoning:
BASE RATES (source winter_base: ERA5-Land at the point, under the exact definitions):
- 1991-2020: 40% of winters had a colder-than-normal DJF and 43% a cold spell.
- Last 15 winters: 27% and 40%.
- All winters since 1950/51: 57% and 61%, inflated by the colder decades.

I start from 1991-2020 because the normal (3.97 °C) is defined on it, then shade towards the last 15 winters. The trend is about 0.32 °C per decade, and the CET had April-September 2026 ranked 362nd-367th warmest of 368. Starting odds: 33% for a cold DJF and 42% for a spell.

1) STRATOSPHERIC VORTEX: +2 on DJF, +5 on the spell.

Strength now:
- The 60°N 10 hPa wind is 12.3 m/s (ECMWF analysis, 31 October).
- Severe-weather.eu's climatology since 1958 puts that below the 10th percentile (17.0 m/s) and just above the record minimum (11.0). Weatheriscool's ERA5 weakest for the date is 11.6 m/s (2016).
- NASA's last analysed day (28 October, 15.8 m/s) sat at the 10th-30th percentile. The 50 hPa wind was already below its 10th percentile.

Reversal shares, from the numeric member counts:
- ECMWF ENS: 100% of members ever easterly, median first reversal 5 November, 98% easterly on 8-10 November, still 39% on 14 November, lowest member -10.0 m/s.
- GEPS: 100%, still 43% easterly on 16 November.
- GEFS (00Z): 90%, with a second dip to 55% on 12 November.
- AIFS ENS (machine learning): 51%, peaking at 37% on one day.
- Weatheriscool's 69% for ECMWF and severe-weather.eu's 59% for AIFS are other runs or windows; I use the numeric shares.

Deterministic runs, an early signal only:
- ECMWF HRES is easterly from 5 to 12 November, down to -4.3 m/s.
- GFS and GEM reverse on 4-5 November.
- UKMO bottoms at +1.1 m/s.
- The machine-learning AIFS deterministic stays westerly (lowest +3.6 m/s), the outlier against the physics models.
- GEOS-FP, which scores the event, forecasts easterly from 5 November and -5.0 m/s on 8 November.

My reading of ECMWF's 46-day spaghetti chart (30 October run):
- members below zero from about 4 to 20 November, mean lowest about -2 to -3 m/s, one member near -11 m/s;
- recovery to about 30 m/s by 27 November and about 42 m/s by 14 December, against a model-climate mean of 32 m/s;
- a few members fall back to 12-19 m/s by mid-December.

The weekly 10 hPa temperature maps:
- 2-9 November: warmth over Siberia and the pole.
- 16-23 November: warm over Canada and Greenland, cold over Scandinavia and the Barents Sea.
- 30 November-7 December: a cold pole again.

Shape: a split-type wave 2 first, then a displacement.
- Wave 2 peaks at 578-607 m on 1-2 November in every model.
- Its ridges tilt west with height by 29-43°, with the 500 hPa ridge at 34-51°E (the Urals) and its partner near Alaska. That is split structure.
- Wave 1 then grows to 758-794 m by 12-15 November (HRES, GFS, AIFS).
- The hebweather ECMWF centroid sits at 59.6-62.6°N to 10 November.
- The ECMWF ENS-mean 10 hPa maps (31 October run): a stretched comma from Canada to Scandinavia on 5 November, a crescent over Greenland and Scandinavia on 10 November, and a vortex centred near Scandinavia on 15 November.
- No GFS or AIFS hemispheric map was readable this run, so their shapes come from the wave numbers. Both models show the same wave-2-then-wave-1 sequence.

Depth, on two measures that disagree:
- The 50 hPa wind stays westerly: ECMWF ENS 2% of members ever easterly, GEFS 0%, AIFS ENS 0%, AIGEFS 3%. The GFS section takes easterlies down only to 30 hPa, on 5 November. Read alone, that would make the event shallow.
- The polar cap says deep:
  - 100 hPa is at +1.76 sd now.
  - Ensemble-mean peaks: ECMWF ENS +2.23, AIFS ENS +2.39, GEFS +2.08, GEPS +2.28 sd.
  - 100% of members in all four ensembles exceed +1 sd.
- By the cap rule I call it deep and coupling.

Coupling to the surface is stronger than last run:
- The ECMWF HRES 500 hPa cap peaks at +0.94 sd on 7 November (last run +0.75).
- The GFS 500 hPa cap reaches +1.29 sd, and its section has the 1000 hPa cap at +0.86 sd on 7 November (last run about +0.5).

Persistence is mixed. Share of members still above +1 sd at 100 hPa on 14 November:
- ECMWF ENS 45%;
- AIFS ENS 84%;
- GEPS 52%;
- GEFS 16%.

Warning signs and the recovery:
- The 10 hPa polar-cap temperature rises only 4-6 °C. This is a dynamical shove of a young vortex, not a classic 20 °C warming.
- The 100 hPa heat flux was 46-47 K m/s on 29 October and about 40 on 3 November. NASA's 45-day mean is above its 90th percentile.
- It collapses to 4-12 K m/s by 10-11 November, with later upticks only to 12-17. That lull drives the rebuild.

What ties it together: this is a bottom-up event.
- AER calls the Ural-Scandinavian block a record. With Barents-Kara water at +2.0 °C (88% of cells more than 1 °C above normal), it pumped wave 2 into a vortex that is only just forming.
- Mid-winter SSWs can steer the surface for 6-8 weeks because the vortex recovers slowly then. In November the vortex recovers quickly, and the westerly QBO speeds that up.
- So the likely response window is about 10 November to early December, mostly outside DJF.
- I raise the DJF credit to +2 (from +1) because the reversal is longer and the surface coupling stronger in this run. The 100 hPa cap near +1 sd in about half of the ECMWF and GEPS members in mid-November could carry into early December.

- Eastward travel to phases 6-7 by mid-November would favour a negative NAO in late November.

- Eurasian weekly extent 4.58 against 5.96 million km² normal (rank 46 of 60).

- Stockholm: 8%.

Met Office (to 28 November): fog and frost under high pressure, then changeable, near or slightly above normal, with lows steered south. I agree. AER (26 October): an unprecedented early weak vortex and further disruption into December. I agree on the vortex but not on December.

Polar vortex strength: zonal-mean zonal wind at 60°N (m/s, daily UTC mean, positive = westerly) at 10 hPa (the standard SSW level: a reversal to easterly is a major sudden stratospheric warming) and 50 hPa (lower stratosphere), per model; ensembles give mean/p10/p90/min across members and the % of members easterly. Early-warning signs from the single runs: polar_cap_t10 = area-mean temperature over 60-90°N at 10 hPa (°C; a jump of 20 °C or more in a few days is a sudden warming under way), heat_flux_100 = eddy heat flux v'T' around 60°N at 100 hPa (K m/s; sustained high values push wave energy up and tend to weaken the vortex 1-2 weeks later), waves_10hPa = amplitude in metres of zonal wavenumber 1 and 2 in the 10 hPa geopotential height around 60°N (wave 1 growing to well over 1000 m means the vortex is being displaced off the pole; wave 2 growing to several hundred metres means it is being stretched towards a split; in winter a few hundred metres each is ordinary; waves_vs_season places today against this season's analysed days). wave2_by_level gives, per single run and day, the longitude (°E, 0-180; the second ridge is 180° further east) of the wave-2 ridges in the 60°N height at 500, 100 and 10 hPa, their amplitudes, and the tilt (10 hPa ridge minus 500 hPa ridge): a ridge that shifts west with height (negative tilt, e.g. 45°E at 500, 29°E at 100, 6°E at 10 hPa) with ridges near the Urals and Alaska is the structure of a split. For ensembles, pct_members_ever_easterly is the share of members that reverse on any day of the run (the SSW probability for that window; the per-day share understates it) and reversal_median_date the typical timing. Days before 2026-10-31 are analysis.

periods.text: High pressure will dominate across the UK early in this period, bringing a lot of dry weather. Some places may start foggy, mainly in the north, this slow to clear and possibly even lingering all day. Elsewhere, cloud amounts will be variable, but there should be some sunshine. Cloud is likely to be thick enough at times for a few mainly light showers or some drizzle though. For most, temperatures are likely to be close to normal, though it will be chilly where any fog lingers, and in the breezier south. Some overnight frost is likely where skies are clear and winds remain light. As we head into the following week, there are signs that more unsettled but potentially milder weather may return, but confidence surrounding this change is low.

During the second half of November, there is an increasing chance of changeable or more unsettled conditions developing, which would mean spells of rain and the potential for strong winds at times. The extent and location of the wettest and/or windiest areas are very uncertain at this range, with the wettest and windiest weather probably towards the north and west, but there are hints that overall the south may be wetter than normal whilst the northwest is a little drier than normal, suggesting the possibility that areas of low pressure may be steered further south than normal. Overall, temperatures will probably be near or a little above normal, although brief colder interludes are also possible with some overnight frost.
